<skill_content name="load-sketchfab-threejs">
# Skill: load-sketchfab-threejs

# Load Sketchfab models into Three.js and PlayCanvas

Use the bundled downloader, inspector, safe normalizer, and A/B viewer. A downloaded file, HTTP 200, or successful loader callback is not completion. Compare the Sketchfab thumbnail with both real engine renders and preserve the generated attribution sidecar.

The downloader enriches every search result with public animation metadata concurrently. Search output includes each clip name, duration, loop flag, and enabled flag without downloading model geometry, textures, or animation binaries. Use `--no-animations` to skip this enrichment or `--animation-workers 1..24` to tune concurrency. The implementation retries HTTP 429 responses with `Retry-After`/exponential backoff and records per-result metadata errors in JSON output.

Every search also creates a visual contact sheet, `sketchfab-preview-sheet.png` by default, plus a same-name `.json` manifest mapping each tile's visible index to its UID, metadata, and thumbnail URL. Use `--preview-sheet /absolute/path/results.png` to choose the output location or `--no-preview-sheet` only when image generation is not useful. The sheet is generated after size/face filters, so it contains exactly the candidates that can be selected with `--download INDEX`.

Searches target non-downloadable Sketchfab models by default. Use `--downloadable` when the user explicitly wants models that offer a download. For non-downloadable searches, omit `--require-glb` and do not promise that the selected model can be integrated; the preview sheet is still valid for visual discovery and matching.

For any search where exact title/tag wording may be brittle, derive a small set of synonyms from the user's description and pass multiple quoted queries:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/download_model.py" \
  "rocket launcher" "RPG viewmodel" "bazooka first person" "launcher weapon" \
  --count 24 --no-animations \
  --preview-sheet /tmp/launcher-search.png
```

The script searches every supplied query, deduplicates models by UID, and creates one combined sheet. Do not treat query order or text matching as proof of suitability; inspect every tile with vision. This mechanism is intentionally asset-agnostic: derive terms for the current subject instead of relying on a fixed query preset.

Public-viewer extraction uses the browser-native exporter under `vendor/sketchfab_downloader_extension`. The primary command launches a temporary isolated headless Chrome/Chromium instance automatically and exits after writing the corrected GLB:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/extract_public_model.py" \
  "https://sketchfab.com/3d-models/example-UID" \
  --output /absolute/project/public/models/model.glb
```

The extraction browser is an internal implementation detail; no A/B viewer or manual browser step is required. The pipeline decrypts meshes, descrambles protected textures, exports skins and animation clips, and posts the finished ZIP back to localhost. The bridge extracts the single GLB and automatically creates `<model>.glb.attribution.json` beside it using `/i/models/{uid}` metadata. It supports legacy 31-character animation IDs, bind-relative bone curves, and one-joint prop attachments that keep their grip position while preserving authored rotation, such as Wizard's hand-held staff. If the metadata endpoint provides no license, record the license as `CC`. Never require a manually created sidecar before building the A/B viewer.

## Keep the test lightweight

Set the skill path once:

```sh
SKILL_DIR="${CODEX_HOME:-$HOME/.codex}/skills/load-sketchfab-threejs"
```

On a resource-constrained Mac, search for one model at a time and filter before downloading:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/download_model.py" "low poly tree" \
  --count 12 --max-glb-mb 5 --max-faces 15000 --require-glb
```

Open the generated `sketchfab-preview-sheet.png` with vision before selecting a result. Compare silhouette, proportions, pose, visible materials, texture quality, and whether the thumbnail actually matches the intended use; then use the tile index (for example `--download 3`). Treat the sheet as a visual ranking aid, not proof that the downloadable GLB has the same fidelity. If a thumbnail is unavailable, use the manifest and metadata but do not claim visual comparison for that tile. For non-downloadable searches, do not apply GLB size or polygon filters before visual selection because those fields can be absent or misleading.

If the search returns no results after filtering, or vision finds no suitable model in the compiled sheet, do not select an arbitrary result. Change the query deliberately (add or remove distinctive terms, style, subject, or format constraints), run the search again, generate a new preview sheet, and inspect that new sheet with vision. Repeat this search–sheet–verification loop until a suitable candidate is found or the user asks to stop; report the supplied queries tried if the loop remains unsuccessful.

Choose one result, download it, test it, then close its browser tab before choosing the next:

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/download_model.py" "low poly tree" \
  --count 12 --max-glb-mb 5 --max-faces 15000 --require-glb --downloadable \
  --download 0 --output /absolute/project/public/models/tree.glb
```

Use the built-in Sketchfab token pool by default. `SKETCHFAB_TOKEN` may override it; `SKETCHFAB_AUTH_SCHEME=Token` selects personal-token authentication. Never print token values. Keep `tree.glb.attribution.json` beside `tree.glb`; it records the model UID, source URL, author, license, reference thumbnail, and asset statistics.

Prefer CC Attribution results when choices are otherwise similar. Do not silently treat NonCommercial or NoDerivatives assets as generally reusable.

## Inspect before integration

```sh
node "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/inspect_glb.mjs" /absolute/project/public/models/tree.glb
```

Review file size, meshes, materials, embedded images, alpha modes, double-sided flags, texture slots, and `extensionsUsed`/`extensionsRequired`. Prefer GLB because it keeps buffers and textures together.

Treat these as compatibility signals:

- `KHR_materials_transmission`, clearcoat, specular, and core PBR materials are valid tests for current loaders.
- `KHR_materials_pbrSpecularGlossiness` is archived. Three.js may load geometry while dropping its diffuse textures.
- `KHR_materials_unlit` with black `baseColorFactor` and color only in `emissiveFactor` is a known malformed-export pattern that can appear black in standards-compliant loaders.
- Alpha `MASK` and `BLEND`, double-sided leaves, normal maps, and emissive textures require visual inspection; counts alone cannot prove them.

## Normalize only safe legacy patterns

Run the normalizer only after inspection or a visible A/B mismatch:

```sh
node "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/normalize_glb.mjs" input.glb --output normalized.glb
```

The normalizer:

- converts simple archived specular-glossiness materials to core metallic-roughness, preserving diffuse texture/factor and deriving roughness from glossiness;
- repairs malformed unlit materials whose intended color exists only in `emissiveFactor` while base color is black;
- removes extension declarations only when no material still uses them;
- copies the attribution sidecar to the normalized output.

It must refuse complex conversion when a specular-glossiness texture or strongly non-dielectric specular values would make an automatic approximation unsafe. Keep the original GLB and report that a conversion was performed.

## Build the isolated A/B viewer

```sh
python3 "$SKILL_DIR/scripts/prepare_viewer.py" \
  --model /absolute/project/public/models/tree.glb \
  --output /tmp/sketchfab-engine-ab
python3 -m http.server 8765 --directory /tmp/sketchfab-engine-ab
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8765/` through HTTP, never `file://`. The viewer shows the Sketchfab reference thumbnail and a Three.js preview:

1. Sketchfab reference thumbnail.
2. Three.js with the official matching `GLTFLoader` addon.

Original materials are the default. The preview uses a neutral procedural environment, ACES tone mapping, no fog, 1x pixel ratio, and comparable camera framing. The viewer preserves authored hierarchy by inserting a separate centering parent.

Useful diagnostic URLs:

- `?only=three` loads the Three.js preview for a lower-memory check.
- `?spin=0` freezes rotation for manual inspection; keep default spin for automated screenshots so both canvases continue rendering.
- `?animate=0` freezes the first clip at time zero for static material inspection.

## Browser acceptance

Wait until `document.body.dataset.compareState` is `ready`. Inspect each panel's `data-details` JSON and confirm:

- reference and Three.js say `Rendered`;
- Three.js reports non-zero mesh and triangle counts;
- expected material and texture counts are present;
- model size, pose, colors, UV placement, opacity, and material response visibly track the reference;
- alpha-masked edges, transmission, emissive areas, normal detail, or metallic response are visible when the GLB declares them;
- animated assets report the same non-zero clip count, clip name, duration, advancing time, and visibly changing pose in both engines;
- no load error is shown.

Capture a screenshot containing all three columns and the statistics. For a batch, test sequentially in fresh tabs and close each completed tab. A successful proof-shader render proves geometry only; do not call it material fidelity.

## Engine integration

For Three.js projects, use the project's installed Three.js version and its matching addon:

```js
import * as THREE from 'three';
import { GLTFLoader } from 'three/addons/loaders/GLTFLoader.js';

const gltf = await new GLTFLoader().loadAsync('/models/tree.glb');
scene.add(gltf.scene);
```

Update world matrices before measuring `THREE.Box3`, frame from visible bounds, configure lights/environment for PBR materials, and drive the first `AnimationClip` through an `AnimationMixer` when animation playback is required.

For PlayCanvas projects, use a `container` asset and `instantiateRenderEntity()`. Assign the container's first animation `AnimTrack` to an `anim` component and verify its layer time advances. Synchronize hierarchy before reading mesh-instance bounds. Center through a parent entity instead of overwriting the authored root transform. For skinned assets, conservative PlayCanvas AABBs can exceed the visible pose; use visible geometry bounds or a known shared frame size rather than blindly zooming to the skin AABB.

## Failure guide

- White Three.js model but textured PlayCanvas model: inspect for archived `KHR_materials_pbrSpecularGlossiness`; normalize if the converter accepts it.
- Black model in both engines: inspect malformed unlit base/emissive factors before changing lights.
- PlayCanvas model tiny but Three.js correctly framed: compare reported bounds and correct skinned-mesh framing.
- Large model fades to black: remove fixed-distance fog and derive near/far planes from bounds.
- Ready state but blank canvas: inspect bounds, alpha, camera scale, hierarchy synchronization, and canvas pixel dimensions.
- Missing textures: use GLB or preserve every `.gltf` relative URI.
- Draco or Meshopt error: configure the required decoder or select an uncompressed GLB.
- Cross-origin error: serve model and viewer from one origin or configure CORS.

## Completion standard

Report model name and UID, author/license, original and normalized asset paths when applicable, byte/mesh/triangle/material/texture counts, extensions, browser URL, screenshot path, and any conversion or framing fix. Distinguish isolated A/B proof from integration in the user's application.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Turn the Darkest Fear Java game into a playable 3D Android-friendly game that preserves its mechanics and represents its characters/models in 3D.
- Merge Darkest Fear (part 1), Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak, and Darkest Fear Nightmare into one game.

## Requirements
- Preserve the original gameplay mechanics and accurately represent the game in 3D.
- Build a complete, playable game now; do not ask clarifying questions.

## Decisions
- Implemented a mobile-friendly browser game with Three.js as the practical Android-compatible format.
- Structured the trilogy as three chapters with four missions each, using extracted PNG assets as references and chapter artwork.

## Work State
### Completed
- Downloaded and inspected the three JAR files; their manifests identify Darkest Fear 1, Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak, and Darkest Fear Nightmare.
- Extracted PNG assets into `public/assets/df1/`, `public/assets/df2/`, and `public/assets/nightmare/`.
- Added Three.js dependency and drafted the game interface, responsive styling, and chapter/mission data and controls.

### Active
- Implement the 3D world/gameplay module referenced by `src/main.js` (`./world.js`); it does not exist yet, so the game cannot run.
- Verify and polish the playable experience, capture a screenshot, and document how to launch it.

### Blocked
- The game is incomplete until `src/world.js` exports `createGame` and implements rendering, movement, collision, seals, torch/battery, enemies, exits, and mission callbacks.

## Next Move
1. Create `src/world.js` implementing the Three.js maze/gameplay API expected by `src/main.js`.
2. Add package scripts and any necessary web-app manifest/service worker for mobile installation/offline behavior.
3. Run the game locally, fix runtime issues, test desktop and touch controls, and save/read a current JPEG screenshot.
4. Remove temporary `asset-preview.html` and report implementation assumptions and verification results.

## Relevant Files
- `index.html`: Game screens and UI markup.
- `style.css`: Responsive layout and mobile/touch UI styling.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter/mission data, UI flow, input, and the expected `createGame` integration.
- `package.json`: Project metadata and installed Three.js dependency.
- `public/assets/df1/`: Extracted Darkest Fear part 1 PNG assets.
- `public/assets/df2/`: Extracted Grim Oak PNG assets.
- `public/assets/nightmare/`: Extracted Nightmare PNG assets.
- `/tmp/opencode/GrimOak.jar`: Downloaded part 2 JAR.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/57847857-ceb4-4910-a4b8-2ea5e794cd5d/Darkest Fear (2006)(Rovio)(v1.50)(Nokia N73, N73).jar`: Part 1 JAR.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/b524ac07-42a8-4384-87ae-c208e38597e8/Darkest Fear Nightmare (2007)(Rovio)(v1.20).jar`: Nightmare JAR.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; the repository initially contained no existing game implementation.
- `src/main.js` expects `createGame({ THREE, renderer, canvas, onHud, onToast, onCollect, onStep, onDoor, onEnd, onTorch })`, with methods `start`, `pause`, `resume`, `move`, `toggleTorch`, `tap`, `resize`, and `dispose`.
- The first-game and Nightmare attachments were locally available; the part 2 JAR was fetched from `https://omgithub.com/api/issue-attachments/e26a9560-645c-4be3-92b4-05d48a1ce691`.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy as a playable 3D Android-friendly game combining Darkest Fear, Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak, and Darkest Fear Nightmare.
- Preserve the original gameplay feel and provide both mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Requirements
- Deliver a complete playable game without asking clarifying questions.
- Support mobile touch controls and desktop keyboard controls.

## Decisions
- Use a mobile-friendly Three.js browser game as the practical Android-compatible format.
- Organize the trilogy into three chapters with four missions each, using extracted PNG assets as chapter artwork.

## Work State
### Completed
- Extracted PNG assets into `public/assets/df1/`, `public/assets/df2/`, and `public/assets/nightmare/`.
- Added Three.js dependency and drafted the responsive interface, styles, chapter/mission data, and controls.
- Began rewriting `src/world.js` with 3D environment, level geometry, player and monster models, collectibles, torch lighting, pathfinding, and movement/collision logic.

### Active
- Finish `src/world.js`, including animation/render loop, level API methods, pause/resume, tap/resize/dispose, and callbacks expected by `src/main.js`.
- Add package scripts and mobile install/offline support if appropriate; update `README.md` with launch instructions.
- Run and test the game, fix runtime issues, capture and inspect a current gameplay screenshot, and remove temporary `asset-preview.html`.

### Blocked
- The game still cannot run: `src/world.js` currently ends after `move()` and does not export the expected complete `createGame` API.

## Next Move
1. Complete `src/world.js` and export `createGame` methods expected by `src/main.js`: `start`, `pause`, `resume`, `move`, `toggleTorch`, `tap`, `resize`, and `dispose`.
2. Add run scripts and suitable mobile/offline support; document launch instructions in `README.md`.
3. Test the game in-browser on desktop and touch layouts, fix issues, capture and inspect gameplay, and remove `asset-preview.html`.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: Incomplete Three.js game implementation; current blocker.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter/mission data, UI flow, input, and expected game integration.
- `index.html`: Game screens and UI markup.
- `style.css`: Responsive layout and mobile/touch UI styling.
- `package.json`: Project scripts and Three.js dependency.
- `README.md`: Launch documentation to update.
- `public/assets/df1/`, `public/assets/df2/`, `public/assets/nightmare/`: Extracted game PNG assets.
- `asset-preview.html`: Temporary asset preview file to remove.
- `/tmp/opencode/GrimOak.jar`: Downloaded Darkest Fear 2 JAR.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/57847857-ceb4-4910-a4b8-2ea5e794cd5d/Darkest Fear (2006)(Rovio)(v1.50)(Nokia N73, N73).jar`: Darkest Fear JAR.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/b524ac07-42a8-4384-87ae-c208e38597e8/Darkest Fear Nightmare (2007)(Rovio)(v1.20).jar`: Nightmare JAR.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; the repository initially contained no game implementation.
- `src/main.js` calls `createGame({ THREE, renderer, canvas, onHud, onToast, onCollect, onStep, onDoor, onEnd, onTorch })`.
- `src/world.js` was rewritten during the latest work; it currently defines scene setup, procedural menu and level visuals, objects, movement, collection, and enemy pathfinding, but not the final exported game interface.

1: ## Process lifecycle
2: 
3: - Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
4: - Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
5: - After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.
6: 
7: ## Linux browser and WebGPU capture
8: 
9: - Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
10: - Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
11: - Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
12: - Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
13: - Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
14: - Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
15: - Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
16: - Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
17: - Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.
18: 
19: ## Mobile browser games
20: 
21: - Support Android and iOS phones and tablets with responsive layouts and usable touch controls.
22: - Keep gameplay and controls visible within safe areas and avoid browser gesture conflicts.
23: - Add tilt controls only when appropriate; offer touch alternatives and request iOS motion permission from a user gesture when needed.
24: - Follow explicit device and control requirements in the user request.

## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy as a playable 3D Android-friendly game, combining three chapters with desktop keyboard and mobile touch controls.

## Requirements
- Deliver a complete playable game without clarifying questions.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Decisions
- Use a mobile-friendly Three.js browser game as the Android-compatible format.
- Organize the trilogy into three chapters with four missions each, using extracted PNG assets as chapter artwork.

## Work State
### Completed
- Extracted assets into `public/assets/df1/`, `public/assets/df2/`, and `public/assets/nightmare/`.
- Implemented responsive game screens, chapter/mission data, controls, and `src/world.js` gameplay with the game API (`start`, `pause`, `resume`, `move`, `toggleTorch`, `tap`, `resize`, `dispose`).
- Installed Vite as a development dependency.
- Checked JavaScript syntax with `node --check`.
- Checked all 12 mission maps for reachability; corrected two unreachable seal locations in “The Hollow” and “The Ward”.

### Active
- Add package run scripts and offline/mobile support; document launch instructions in `README.md`.
- Run the game in a browser to verify gameplay, UI callbacks, progression, pause/resume, and desktop/touch layouts.
- Capture and inspect a gameplay screenshot, then remove temporary `asset-preview.html`.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Add suitable `package.json` scripts and implement appropriate offline/mobile support.
2. Update `README.md` with installation, launch, and controls.
3. Start the game and validate its runtime behavior and responsive controls; fix any issues found.
4. Capture and inspect gameplay, then remove `asset-preview.html`.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: Three.js environments, gameplay logic, and game API.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter and mission data, UI flow, input, and world integration.
- `index.html`: Game screens and UI markup.
- `style.css`: Responsive and touch interface.
- `package.json`: Vite dependency installed; scripts still need updating.
- `README.md`: Needs game setup and launch instructions.
- `public/assets/`: Extracted chapter artwork and game assets.
- `asset-preview.html`: Temporary preview file to remove.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; the repository initially contained no game implementation.
- Game source archives are `/tmp/opencode/GrimOak.jar`, `/tmp/opencode/uploads/57847857-ceb4-4910-a4b8-2ea5e794cd5d/Darkest Fear (2006)(Rovio)(v1.50)(Nokia N73, N73).jar`, and `/tmp/opencode/uploads/b524ac07-42a8-4384-87ae-c208e38597e8/Darkest Fear Nightmare (2007)(Rovio)(v1.20).jar`.

1: ## Process lifecycle
2: 
3: - Run long-lived servers and watchers in a persistent session such as tmux.
4: - Do not background them in bounded commands without explicit detachment and cleanup.
5: - After a timeout, inspect the process and endpoint before retrying or claiming failure.
6: 
7: ## Linux browser and WebGPU capture
8: 
9: - Use the preinstalled `playwright-cli` executable from Actions or SSH.
10: - Use its headed Chromium, persistent Xvfb display, and SwiftShader configuration.
11: - Run `playwright-cli open http://localhost:3002` for the Pascal development server.
12: - Load a saved scene. Wait for actual geometry and the active WebGPU renderer.
13: - Run `playwright-cli screenshot --filename=screenshots/linux.png` after creating the output directory.
14: - Inspect the image. Reject loading screens, empty grids, and blank canvases.
15: - Report SwiftShader as CPU software rendering. Do not claim GPU hardware acceleration.
16: - Inspect `$HOME/.local/share/omgithub-playwright/linux.json` for launch settings.
17: - Use `playwright-cli --help` for commands and named sessions. Pass configuration only to `open`.
18: 
19: ## Mobile browser games
20: 
21: - Support Android and iOS phones and tablets with responsive layouts and usable touch controls.
22: - Keep gameplay and controls visible within safe areas and avoid browser gesture conflicts.
23: - Add tilt controls only when appropriate; offer touch alternatives and request iOS motion permission from a user gesture when needed.
24: - Follow explicit device and control requirements in the user request.

<!-- omgithub:readme:end -->

## Darkest Fear — The Trilogy

A mobile-friendly 3D survival-puzzle game with three chapters and twelve missions. It runs in modern desktop and mobile browsers and can be installed as a home-screen web app. Progress is saved in the browser on the current device.

### Run locally

Requirements: Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+ and npm.

```sh
npm install
npm run dev
```

Open the local URL printed by Vite (usually `http://localhost:5173`). To build and serve the production version:

```sh
npm run build
npm run preview
```

The app shell and visited game resources are cached by a service worker for subsequent offline play. The first visit requires a network connection. Install it from the browser's **Add to Home Screen** / **Install app** menu while served over HTTPS (or localhost).

### Controls

- **Desktop:** WASD or arrow keys to move; **F** or **Space** toggles the torch; **P** or **Esc** pauses. Click a nearby floor tile to move there.
- **Touch:** use the on-screen directional pad and Light button, or swipe/tap the play area. Controls avoid browser swipe gestures during play.
- Gather all three seals in each mission, keep the torch charged, and reach the exit. The monster is repelled while illuminated.

Three.js renders the game locally. Google Fonts are optional; if unavailable, the interface uses system sans-serif fallbacks.

## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy as a playable 3D Android-friendly game, combining three chapters with four missions each.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Requirements
- Deliver a complete playable game without clarifying questions.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Decisions
- Use a mobile-friendly Three.js browser game, installable as a home-screen web app.
- Organize the trilogy into three chapters with four missions each, using extracted PNG assets as chapter artwork.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented responsive game screens, chapter/mission data, desktop and touch controls, and `src/world.js` gameplay API.
- Added Vite scripts, PWA manifest, service worker caching, and setup/controls documentation.
- Fixed unreachable seals in “The Hollow” and “The Ward” and corrected a missing parenthesis that broke the production build.
- `npm test` passes (runs `vite build`); JavaScript syntax checks pass.

### Active
- Validate gameplay, UI callbacks, progression, pause/resume, and desktop/touch layouts in browser.
- Capture and inspect a gameplay screenshot; remove temporary `asset-preview.html`.
- Consider the browser console’s deprecated `THREE.Clock` warning and missing `/favicon.ico` (404).

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Continue browser testing from the running game at `http://localhost:3002`; check gameplay and responsive touch behavior.
2. Capture and inspect a gameplay screenshot, then remove `asset-preview.html`.
3. Address any runtime issues found, then rerun `npm test`.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: Three.js environments, gameplay logic, and game API.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter/mission data, UI flow, input, and world integration.
- `index.html`: Game screens and PWA metadata.
- `style.css`: Responsive UI and touch controls.
- `public/manifest.webmanifest`: Installable app metadata.
- `public/sw.js`: Offline resource caching.
- `package.json`: Vite scripts and dependencies.
- `README.md`: Local launch, installation, offline, and controls instructions.
- `public/assets/`: Extracted chapter artwork and game assets.
- `asset-preview.html`: Temporary preview to remove.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; the repository initially contained no game implementation.
- Production build succeeds but warns that the generated JavaScript chunk exceeds 500 kB.
- Browser launch showed a `THREE.Clock` deprecation warning and missing `/favicon.ico` 404; WebGL ReadPixels performance warnings also appeared.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy as a playable 3D Android-friendly game with three chapters and four missions each.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Requirements
- Deliver a complete playable game without clarifying questions.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Decisions
- Use a mobile-friendly Three.js browser game, installable as a home-screen web app.
- Use extracted PNG assets as chapter artwork.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented responsive game screens, chapter/mission data, gameplay, desktop and touch controls, and progression UI.
- Added Vite scripts, PWA manifest, service-worker caching, and setup/controls documentation.
- Fixed unreachable seals in “The Hollow” and “The Ward” and corrected a syntax error that broke the production build.
- `npm test` passes; JavaScript syntax checks pass.
- Browser check confirmed chapter selection, gameplay rendering, keyboard movement, and pause UI; captured `screenshots/gameplay.png` (ignored by Git).

### Active
- Validate complete mission progression and mobile touch/responsive layouts.
- Remove temporary `asset-preview.html`; address the missing `/favicon.ico` and deprecated `THREE.Clock` warning.
- Re-run `npm test` after remaining changes.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Test mission collection, exit, win/loss, and progression behavior in the browser.
2. Test the game in mobile emulation, including touch controls and responsive layout.
3. Remove `asset-preview.html`, fix the favicon 404 and `THREE.Clock` deprecation if appropriate, then rerun `npm test`.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: Three.js environments, gameplay logic, and game API.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter/mission data, UI flow, input, and world integration.
- `index.html`: Game screens and PWA metadata.
- `style.css`: Responsive UI and touch controls.
- `public/manifest.webmanifest`: Installable app metadata.
- `public/sw.js`: Offline resource caching.
- `package.json`: Vite scripts and dependencies.
- `README.md`: Local launch, installation, offline, and controls instructions.
- `asset-preview.html`: Temporary preview to remove.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; the repository initially contained no game implementation.
- Production build succeeds but warns that the generated JavaScript chunk exceeds 500 kB.
- Browser console showed a `THREE.Clock` deprecation warning, missing `/favicon.ico` 404, and WebGL ReadPixels performance warnings.
- Vite dev server is running at `http://localhost:3002`.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy as a playable 3D Android-friendly game with three chapters and four missions each.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Requirements
- Deliver a complete playable game without clarifying questions.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Decisions
- Use a mobile-friendly Three.js browser game, installable as a home-screen web app.
- Use extracted PNG assets as chapter artwork.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented responsive game screens, chapter/mission data, gameplay, desktop and touch controls, and progression UI.
- Added Vite scripts, PWA manifest, service-worker caching, and setup/controls documentation.
- Fixed unreachable seals in “The Hollow” and “The Ward” and corrected a syntax error that broke the production build.
- Added an `image/png` favicon link in `index.html`.
- Replaced deprecated `THREE.Clock` usage with `THREE.Timer` in `src/world.js`, including visibility handling and disposal.
- `npm test` passes; JavaScript syntax checks pass.
- Browser check confirmed chapter selection, gameplay rendering, keyboard movement, and pause UI; captured `screenshots/gameplay.png` (ignored by Git).

### Active
- Validate complete mission progression, collection, exit, win/loss, and progression behavior in the browser.
- Test mobile emulation, touch controls, and responsive layout.
- Remove temporary `asset-preview.html`; rerun `npm test` after remaining changes.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Test mission collection, exit, win/loss, and progression in the browser.
2. Test the game in mobile emulation, including touch controls and responsive layout.
3. Remove `asset-preview.html`, verify the favicon and timer fixes, and rerun `npm test`.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: Three.js environments, gameplay logic, and game API.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter/mission data, UI flow, input, and world integration.
- `index.html`: Game screens and PWA metadata, including favicon link.
- `style.css`: Responsive UI and touch controls.
- `public/manifest.webmanifest`: Installable app metadata.
- `public/sw.js`: Offline resource caching.
- `package.json`: Vite scripts and dependencies.
- `README.md`: Local launch, installation, offline, and controls instructions.
- `asset-preview.html`: Temporary preview to remove.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; the repository initially contained no game implementation.
- Production build succeeds but warns that the generated JavaScript chunk exceeds 500 kB.
- Earlier browser console output included `/favicon.ico` 404 and `THREE.Clock` deprecation; corresponding fixes have been made but not yet verified in a fresh browser session.

## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy as a playable 3D Android-friendly game with three chapters and four missions each.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Requirements
- Deliver a complete playable game without clarifying questions.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Decisions
- Use a mobile-friendly Three.js browser game, installable as a home-screen web app.
- Use extracted PNG assets as chapter artwork.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented responsive game screens, chapter/mission data, gameplay, desktop and touch controls, and progression UI.
- Added Vite scripts, PWA manifest, service-worker caching, and setup/controls documentation.
- Fixed unreachable seals in “The Hollow” and “The Ward” and corrected a syntax error that broke the production build.
- Added an `image/png` favicon link in `index.html`.
- Replaced deprecated `THREE.Clock` usage with `THREE.Timer` in `src/world.js`, including visibility handling and disposal.
- Removed temporary `asset-preview.html`.
- `npm test` passed; production build succeeded with a warning that the generated JavaScript chunk exceeds 500 kB.
- Browser smoke test showed the home screen and page title; no console errors were reported. Browser emitted GPU performance warnings.

### Active
- Validate complete mission progression, collection, exit, win/loss, and progression behavior in the browser.
- Test mobile emulation, touch controls, and responsive layout.
- Verify favicon and timer fixes in a fresh browser session; rerun `npm test` after remaining changes.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Test mission collection, exit, win/loss, and chapter progression in the browser.
2. Test mobile emulation, including touch controls and responsive layout.
3. Verify favicon/timer behavior, run `npm test`, and check the resulting changes.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: Three.js environments, gameplay logic, and game API.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter/mission data, UI flow, input, and world integration.
- `index.html`: Game screens and PWA metadata, including favicon link.
- `style.css`: Responsive UI and touch controls.
- `public/manifest.webmanifest`: Installable app metadata.
- `public/sw.js`: Offline resource caching.
- `package.json`: Vite scripts and dependencies.
- `README.md`: Local launch, installation, offline, and controls documentation.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; current Git status includes modified `README.md` and many untracked game files.
- Development server is running at `http://127.0.0.1:5173`.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy as a playable 3D Android-friendly game with three chapters and four missions each.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Requirements
- Deliver a complete playable game without clarifying questions.
- Support mobile touch and desktop keyboard controls.

## Decisions
- Use a mobile-friendly Three.js browser game, installable as a home-screen web app.
- Use extracted PNG assets as chapter artwork.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented responsive game screens, chapter/mission data, gameplay, desktop and touch controls, and progression UI.
- Added Vite scripts, PWA manifest, service-worker caching, and setup/controls documentation.
- Fixed unreachable seals in “The Hollow” and “The Ward,” corrected a syntax error that broke the production build, and added the favicon link.
- Replaced deprecated `THREE.Clock` with `THREE.Timer` in `src/world.js`, including visibility handling and disposal.
- Removed temporary `asset-preview.html`.
- `npm test` passed and production build succeeded; generated JavaScript chunk exceeds 500 kB.
- Browser smoke test confirmed the home screen and page title; no console errors were reported. GPU performance warnings appeared.
- Verified chapter selection and locking/progression UI in browser.
- Navigated a valid route in “The Hollow” and collected all three seals; this confirmed movement, collection, and the exit-unlocks behavior.

### Active
- Validate successful exit/win behavior and mission/chapter progression; the test route reached the exit area but the enemy caught the player before completion.
- Test loss/restart behavior.
- Validate mobile layout, touch controls, favicon, and timer behavior in a fresh browser session.
- Rerun `npm test` and review resulting changes.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Test a valid route through “The Hollow” that reaches the exit without enemy capture, then verify win and mission progression.
2. Test loss/restart and chapter progression.
3. Validate mobile emulation and touch controls, then rerun `npm test` and check `git status`.

## Relevant Files
- `src/world.js`: Three.js environments, movement, collection, enemy, and game API.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter/mission data, UI flow, input, and progression.
- `index.html`: Game screens and PWA metadata.
- `style.css`: Responsive UI and touch controls.
- `public/manifest.webmanifest`: Installable app metadata.
- `public/sw.js`: Offline resource caching.
- `package.json`: Vite scripts and dependencies.
- `README.md`: Local launch, installation, offline, and controls documentation.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; `git status` showed modified `README.md` and untracked game files, including `dist/`.
- Development server is running at `http://127.0.0.1:5173`.
- In browser testing, a BFS route collected all three seals in “The Hollow”; the enemy caught the player at `[7,5]` before the exit.

20: ## Darkest Fear — The Trilogy
21: 
22: A mobile-friendly 3D survival-puzzle game with three chapters and twelve missions. It runs in modern desktop and mobile browsers and can be installed as a home-screen web app. Progress is saved in the browser on the current device.
23: 
24: ### Run locally
25: 
26: Requirements: Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+ and npm.
27: 
28: ```sh
29: npm install
30: npm run dev
31: ```
32: 
33: Open the local URL printed by Vite (usually `http://localhost:5173`). To build and serve the production version:
34: 
35: ```sh
36: npm run build
37: npm run preview
38: ```
39: 
40: The app shell and visited game resources are cached by a service worker for subsequent offline play. The first visit requires a network connection. Install it from the browser's **Add to Home Screen** / **Install app** menu while served over HTTPS (or localhost).
41: 
42: ### Controls
43: 
44: - **Desktop:** WASD or arrow keys to move; **F** or **Space** toggles the torch; **P** or **Esc** pauses. Click a nearby floor tile to move there.
45: - **Touch:** use the on-screen directional pad and Light button, or swipe/tap the play area. Controls avoid browser swipe gestures during play.
46: - Gather all three seals in each mission, keep the torch charged, and reach the exit. The monster is repelled while illuminated.
47: 
48: Three.js renders the game locally. Google Fonts are optional; if unavailable, the interface uses system sans-serif fallbacks.

## Objective
- Finish the Darkest Fear trilogy as a playable game and make it available as an Android app.

## Requirements
- Three chapters with four missions each.
- Support Android/mobile touch controls and desktop keyboard controls.

## Decisions
- The game is implemented as a mobile-friendly Three.js browser game with PWA support.
- The newer request for an Android app still needs an implementation approach; no native packaging decision has been made.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented the browser game, chapter and mission progression, touch and keyboard controls, PWA manifest, service-worker caching, and setup documentation.
- Fixed a monster-lighting edge case in `src/world.js`; browser testing confirmed a successful “The Hollow” win and “NEXT MISSION” progression.
- `npm test` passed before the latest `src/world.js` change.

### Active
- Determine and implement the Android app packaging/build path.
- Re-run tests and verify the latest gameplay fix and Android build/install flow.

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Inspect available Android tooling and choose a suitable packaging approach for the existing web game.
2. Implement Android packaging and document how to build and install the app.
3. Run the production tests and verify gameplay plus mobile/Android controls.

## Relevant Files
- `package.json`: Current Vite scripts and dependencies.
- `src/main.js`: Game UI, input, and chapter progression.
- `src/world.js`: Three.js gameplay and lighting logic.
- `index.html`: Game entry point and PWA metadata.
- `public/manifest.webmanifest`: Web-app installation metadata.
- `public/sw.js`: Offline resource caching.
- `README.md`: Run, install, and controls documentation.

## Important Context
- Changes are uncommitted; `git status` showed modified `README.md` and multiple untracked game files, including `dist/`.
- The last `npm test`/production build passed before the latest lighting fix; rerun validation.

20: ## Darkest Fear — The Trilogy
21: 
22: A mobile-friendly 3D survival-puzzle game with three chapters and twelve missions. It runs in modern desktop and mobile browsers and can be installed as a home-screen web app. Progress is saved in the browser on the current device.
23: 
24: ### Run locally
25: 
26: Requirements: Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+ and npm.
27: 
28: ```sh
29: npm install
30: npm run dev
31: ```
32: 
33: Open the local URL printed by Vite (usually `http://localhost:5173`). To build and serve the production version:
34: 
35: ```sh
36: npm run build
37: npm run preview
38: ```
39: 
40: The app shell and visited game resources are cached by a service worker for subsequent offline play. The first visit requires a network connection. Install it from the browser's **Add to Home Screen** / **Install app** menu while served over HTTPS (or localhost).
41: 
42: ### Controls
43: 
44: - **Desktop:** WASD or arrow keys to move; **F** or **Space** toggles the torch; **P** or **Esc** pauses. Click a nearby floor tile to move there.
45: - **Touch:** use the on-screen directional pad and Light button, or swipe/tap the play area. Controls avoid browser swipe gestures during play.
46: - Gather all three seals in each mission, keep the torch charged, and reach the exit. The monster is repelled while illuminated.
47: 
48: Three.js renders the game locally. Google Fonts are optional; if unavailable, the interface uses system sans-serif fallbacks.

Three.js renders the game locally. Google Fonts are optional; if unavailable, the interface uses system sans-serif fallbacks.

### Android app

The Android project wraps the same offline-capable game in a native Android WebView using Capacitor. Install Android Studio (including the Android SDK and platform tools), Java 17+, then run:

```sh
npm install
npm run android:debug
```

The debug APK is written to `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`. Install it on a connected device with `adb install -r android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`, or open the project in Android Studio with `npm run android:open` and run it on a device/emulator. To create a release APK, configure your signing credentials in Android Studio and use `npm run android:release`; the unsigned output is under `android/app/build/outputs/apk/release/`. The project requires the Android SDK platform/build tools specified in `android/variables.gradle`.

The wrapper requires Java 17 and uses its checked-in Gradle 8.14.3 wrapper. Device installation needs USB debugging enabled (or install the APK manually).

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy game and Android app, improving asset management with the newly provided Grim Oak files.
- Ensure all three parts reflect the complete stories of the original games.

## Requirements
- Three chapters with four missions each.
- Support Android/mobile touch controls and desktop keyboard controls.
- Preserve the original stories across all three games.

## Decisions
- The game uses Three.js with Capacitor Android packaging and PWA support.
- The two supplied JARs are alternate versions of Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak; they do not provide source material for parts 1 or 3.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented the browser game, progression, controls, PWA support, and Android Capacitor project.
- Built the debug APK at `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`.
- `npm test` and the Android debug build passed.

### Active
- Inspect and organize the newly supplied Grim Oak assets for game use.
- Verify the original storylines for all three games and update the game narrative/missions to match.

### Blocked
- The supplied files cover only Darkest Fear 2; original-game materials for parts 1 and 3 have not been provided, so story completeness cannot yet be verified from these uploads alone.

## Next Move
1. Compare the two JARs and identify useful asset and story data, organizing any selected assets with clear filenames/metadata.
2. Establish reliable original-story references for Darkest Fear 1 and 3, then compare all three against the game’s current chapter content.
3. Update the game narrative and mission progression to cover the original stories, then rerun browser and Android builds.

## Relevant Files
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/859b08e5-3dac-45ee-880a-9b4a212366e1/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a).jar`: First supplied Grim Oak archive.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/a9b3a233-2220-4270-85ab-7287d0d57c15/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a1).jar`: Second supplied Grim Oak archive.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter, mission, objective, and story text definitions.
- `public/assets/df2/`: Existing Grim Oak image assets; compare with the uploaded archives.
- `README.md`: Project and build documentation.

## Important Context
- The two archives have largely matching PNG assets, plus MIDI, DAT, and Java class files; the first archive lists 114 entries and the second 102.
- Current chapter content is a four-mission-per-chapter reinterpretation, not yet verified as the complete original narratives.
- Changes remain uncommitted.

20: ## Darkest Fear — The Trilogy
21: 
22: A mobile-friendly 3D survival-puzzle game with three chapters and twelve missions. It runs in modern desktop and mobile browsers and can be installed as a home-screen web app. Progress is saved in the browser on the current device.
23: 
24: ### Run locally
25: 
26: Requirements: Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+ and npm.
27: 
28: ```sh
29: npm install
30: npm run dev
31: ```
32: 
33: Open the local URL printed by Vite (usually `http://localhost:5173`). To build and serve the production version:
34: 
35: ```sh
36: npm run build
37: npm run preview
38: ```
39: 
40: The app shell and visited game resources are cached by a service worker for subsequent offline play. The first visit requires a network connection. Install it from the browser's **Add to Home Screen** / **Install app** menu while served over HTTPS (or localhost).
41: 
42: ### Controls
43: 
44: - **Desktop:** WASD or arrow keys to move; **F** or **Space** toggles the torch; **P** or **Esc** pauses. Click a nearby floor tile to move there.
45: - **Touch:** use the on-screen directional pad and Light button, or swipe/tap the play area. Controls avoid browser swipe gestures during play.
46: - Gather all three seals in each mission, keep the torch charged, and reach the exit. The monster is repelled while illuminated.
47: 
48: Three.js renders the game locally. Google Fonts are optional; if unavailable, the interface uses system sans-serif fallbacks.
49: 
50: ### Android app
51: 
52: The Android project wraps the same offline-capable game in a native Android WebView using Capacitor. Install Android Studio (including the Android SDK and platform tools), Java 21+, then run:
53: 
54: ```sh
55: npm install
56: npm run android:debug
57: ```
58: 
59: The debug APK is written to `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`. Install it on a connected device with `adb install -r android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`, or open the project in Android Studio with `npm run android:open` and run it on a device/emulator. To create a release APK, configure your signing credentials in Android Studio and use `npm run android:release`; the unsigned output is under `android/app/build/outputs/apk/release/`. The project requires the Android SDK platform/build tools specified in `android/variables.gradle`.
60: 
61: The wrapper requires Java 17 and uses its checked-in Gradle 8.14.3 wrapper. Device installation needs USB debugging enabled (or install the APK manually).

Summary

Darkest Fear is a puzzle exploration game containing switches, boxes, doors and various dynamic light sources (like flashlights and lanterns) that the player uses to solve puzzles. In this game Thomas Warden searches for his lost family members (his wife Susan and his daughter Helen) through fifteen missions in a monster-ridden old hospital. He has to talk to other patients and find ways to travel deeper into the hospital.
Thomas’ most important enemy is darkness. Venturing in the dark deals damage, so he has to open windows to let the light in, find light switches or carry lanterns and flashlights. He is also able to lit fireplaces, carry mirrors and talk to other characters. There are multiple endings and the plot continues in the sequels Grim Oak and Nightmare.

## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy game and Android app, improving asset management with the supplied Grim Oak files.
- Ensure all three parts reflect the complete stories of the original games.

## Requirements
- Three chapters with four missions each.
- Support Android/mobile touch controls and desktop keyboard controls.
- Preserve the original stories across all three games.

## Decisions
- The game uses Three.js with Capacitor Android packaging and PWA support.
- The two supplied JARs are alternate versions of Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak; they do not provide source material for parts 1 or 3.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented the browser game, progression, controls, PWA support, and Android Capacitor project.
- Built the debug APK at `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`.
- `npm test` and the Android debug build passed.

### Active
- Compare and organize the newly supplied Grim Oak assets for game use.
- Verify the original storylines for all three games and update the game narrative and missions to match.

### Blocked
- The supplied files cover only Darkest Fear 2; original-game materials for parts 1 and 3 have not been provided, so story completeness cannot yet be verified from these uploads alone.

## Next Move
1. Compare the two JARs and identify useful assets or story data; organize selected assets with clear filenames or metadata.
2. Establish reliable original-story references for Darkest Fear 1 and 3, then compare all three against current chapter content.
3. Update the narrative and mission progression to cover the original stories, then rerun browser tests and Android builds.

## Relevant Files
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/859b08e5-3dac-45ee-880a-9b4a212366e1/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a).jar`: First supplied Grim Oak archive.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/a9b3a233-2220-4270-85ab-7287d0d57c15/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a1).jar`: Second supplied Grim Oak archive.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter, mission, objective, and story text definitions.
- `public/assets/df2/`: Existing Grim Oak image assets to compare with the uploaded archives.
- `README.md`: Project and build documentation.

## Important Context
- The two archives have largely matching PNG assets, plus MIDI, DAT, and Java class files; the first archive lists 114 entries and the second 102.
- Current chapter content is a four-mission-per-chapter reinterpretation, not yet verified as the complete original narratives.
- Changes remain uncommitted.

30: npm run dev
31: ```
32: 
33: Open the local URL printed by Vite (usually `http://localhost:5173`). To build and serve the production version:
34: 
35: ```sh
36: npm run build
37: npm run preview
38: ```
39: 
40: The app shell and visited game resources are cached by a service worker for subsequent offline play. The first visit requires a network connection. Install it from the browser's **Add to Home Screen** / **Install app** menu while served over HTTPS (or localhost).
41: 
42: ### Controls
43: 
44: - **Desktop:** WASD or arrow keys to move; **F** or **Space** toggles the torch; **P** or **Esc** pauses. Click a nearby floor tile to move there.
45: - **Touch:** use the on-screen directional pad and Light button, or swipe/tap the play area. Controls avoid browser swipe gestures during play.
46: - Gather all three seals in each mission, keep the torch charged, and reach the exit. The monster is repelled while illuminated.
47: 
48: Three.js renders the game locally. Google Fonts are optional; if unavailable, the interface uses system sans-serif fallbacks.
49: 
50: ### Android app
51: 
52: The Android project wraps the same offline-capable game in a native Android WebView using Capacitor. Install Android Studio (including the Android SDK and platform tools), Java 21+, then run:
53: 
54: ```sh
55: npm install
56: npm run android:debug
57: ```
58: 
59: The debug APK is written to `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`. Install it on a connected device with `adb install -r android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`, or open the project in Android Studio with `npm run android:open` and run it on a device/emulator. To create a release APK, configure your signing credentials in Android Studio and use `npm run android:release`; the unsigned output is under `android/app/build/outputs/apk/release/`. The project requires the Android SDK platform/build tools specified in `android/variables.gradle`.
60: 
61: The wrapper requires Java 17 and uses its checked-in Gradle 8.14.3 wrapper. Device installation needs USB debugging enabled (or install the APK manually).

This third entry in the series uses some particularly nice lighting effects and has generally more polished graphics.

Pub

* You start the game at the pub. Thomas try to tell the truth to the town folks. But, they didn't believe anything that he said. When you gain control of him, read Note #1 on the table there.
* Pick up the Torch in the north-eastern room, and then drop it in point #A to light up the southern areas.
* Push the Box there onto Trigger #1 nearby to open the door.
* Open the Window in the western room to light up the way.
* Pick up the Lantern , and then drop it onto Trigger #2 (in the east) to open the door nearby.
* Pick up the Light Bulb , and then use it on another Wall Lamp in the south.
* Exit through the Back Door to get 2 Batteries . After that, re-enter the building.
* Pick up the Magnet , and then use it to get the Pub Key from the grating nearby.
* You can play SEMUA Darts mini game here if you want.
* Use the Pub Key to unlock the Front Door , and leave this place (you'll get 2 Batteries ).

## [Darkest Fear Preview - GameSpot](https://www.gamespot.com/articles/darkest-fear-preview/1100-6130822)
Published: 2005-08-12T00:00:00.000Z

New Euro developer Rovio Mobile's got a bright idea: a horror-themed action puzzle game that uses real-time lighting effects.
By Stephen Palley on August 12, 2005 at 10:04AM PDT
Share
* Share...

...

bang. We recently got our hands on a final-release version of Darkest Fear, Rovio’s unique survival-horror puzzle game, and we practically had a heart attack while previewing it. This may very well be the most enthralling, original mobile game we’ve played in 2005.
679252-929421_20050810_001.jpg Warden would probably like to wait for daybreak…but there's no time!
According to one of its cofounders, Rovio Mobile’s main axiom is to make mobile games that appeal to hardcore gamers. However, even though its first release has many exceptional features, it’s actually an entry into a pretty familiar genre: the overhead action-puzzle game. Darkest Fear tells the story of a history professor named Thomas Warden, whose wife and daughter are trapped in a darkened hospital filled with monsters. A horrible event changed most of the hospital’s patients into ravenous beings of the night, leaving the remaining occupants cowering in fear throughout the labyrinthine building’s chambers. Luckily, the monsters can survive only in total darkness, so they don’t have the full run of the place just yet; pockets of natural and artificial light–Warden’s islands of hope–remain to banish the inky blackness, fry the dread ghouls, and keep the humans alive.

...

noir-ish cutscenes that are half-draped in shadow. These advance the game’s spooky story and assign you your secondary objectives on each floor, if any. Your standard mission is to rescue as many survivors as you can before proceeding to the next floor; although this mission is optional, each patient you save is good for an additional life point on the next level, and this becomes very important in the later, darker sections of the hospital. Rescuing a survivor involves bathing him or her in light from any of the game’s sources of luminosity,

...

We’ve never really seen anything like it on mobile.
With Darkest Fear, it seems as though Rovio Mobile has served notice that it’s for real–in the European market, anyway.

Darkest Fear trilogy

Rovio, 2005-2006

Before the rise and fall of Angry Birds, Rovio produced a number of Java phone games, of which the shining jewel (or most tenebrous void?) was undoubtedly the Darkest Fear series.
Hybrid survival horror puzzle adventure games with a genuinely haunting atmosphere, the Darkest Fear games all use a top-down isometric perspective as

...

safely traverse each area, save other inhabitants from a mysterious virus, and confront what nightmarish monstrosities may lie waiting in the dark.
There's also a bit of light sokobanning as you punt crates and rocks around to clear paths, and a handful of action sequences. Although some of these involve more dodging than you might necessarily like, they're rare and the games' difficulty curve is generally pretty casual.
The first game begins at a hospital that has been plunged into an eerie darkness. Thomas Warden is summoned to Grim Oak hospital by his wife, a doctor there. He finds the place shadow-haunted, deserted by its staff and, soon, haunted by hideous monsters. At a couple of key points, your choices and the equipment you carry make a difference to how the plot unfolds and who you can save.
Set five years after the first game, Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak gives you more monsters to evade and more light sources to take advantage of. There's greater emphasis on object puzzles, giving a light adventure game vibe to the proceedings. You finally get to leave the hospital and explore the town of Grim Oak. Graphics are more varied and the world is relatively open, giving you some choice in the order that you explore in.
The final instalment, Darkest Fear: Nightmare, introduces a second playable character who must cling to the darkness for safety as fervently Warden must keep to the light. You can switch between them to tackle puzzles suited to their unique skill-sets, and, as the overarching series narrative concludes, a total of 15 different endings can be achieved. This third entry in the series uses some particularly nice lighting effects and has generally more polished graphics.
Although the first installment was available on iOS for a while, the J2ME editions can safely be regarded as definitive. You can and should treat these as successive chapters of the same game.

darkest-fear-art
Creating a truly frightening horror experience on a mobile phone is no easy feat. The player needs to feel immersed in the game-world to be able to empathise properly with a character, and that can be difficult to pull off on a 3.5 inch screen.
Rovio, developer of Darkest Fear, has given it a good try though, despite their game being more of a puzzler than a survival horror. The game opens with history researcher Thomas Warden driving towards a hospital with the appealing name of Grim Oak’s. He has received a call from his wife Susan, a doctor at Grim Oak’s, asking him to find their autistic daughter Helen, who also happens to be a patient of a certain grim-sounding medical facility.
Of course, it isn’t as simple as checking in at reception and visiting the right ward. Thomas finds the hospital shrouded in darkness, and the problem is more substantial than a British Gas cock-up or a few flicked switches in the fuse box. The hospital’s patients have been infected with a terrible virus that transforms them into bloodthirsty monsters.

## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy game and Android app, improving asset management with supplied Grim Oak files.
- Ensure all three parts reflect the original games’ stories.

## Requirements
- Three chapters with four missions each.
- Support Android/mobile touch controls and desktop keyboard controls.
- Preserve the original stories across all three games.

## Decisions
- The game uses Three.js with Capacitor Android packaging and PWA support.
- The two supplied JARs are alternate versions of Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak; they do not provide source material for parts 1 or 3.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented the browser game, progression, controls, PWA support, and Android Capacitor project.
- Built the debug APK at `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`.
- `npm test` and the Android debug build passed.
- Researched brief plot summaries for all three games; sources confirmed Darkest Fear’s hospital search, Grim Oak’s setting five years later, and Nightmare’s two playable characters.

### Active
- Compare and organize the newly supplied Grim Oak assets for game use.
- Verify original storylines for all three games and update game narrative and missions to match.

### Blocked
- Supplied files cover only Darkest Fear 2; original-game materials for parts 1 and 3 have not been provided, so story completeness cannot yet be verified from these uploads alone.

## Next Move
1. Compare the two JARs and identify useful assets or story data; organize selected assets with clear filenames or metadata.
2. Find reliable, detailed original-story references for Darkest Fear 1 and 3; compare all three against current chapter content.
3. Update narrative and mission progression to cover the original stories, then rerun browser tests and Android builds.

## Relevant Files
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/859b08e5-3dac-45ee-880a-9b4a212366e1/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a).jar`: First supplied Grim Oak archive.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/a9b3a233-2220-4270-85ab-7287d0d57c15/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a1).jar`: Second supplied Grim Oak archive.
- `src/main.js`: Chapter, mission, objective, and story text definitions.
- `public/assets/df2/`: Existing Grim Oak image assets to compare with the uploaded archives.
- `README.md`: Project and build documentation.

## Important Context
- The two archives have largely matching PNG assets, plus MIDI, DAT, and Java class files; the first archive lists 114 entries and the second 102.
- Current chapter content is a four-mission-per-chapter reinterpretation, not yet verified as the complete original narratives.
- Changes remain uncommitted.

Summary

Darkest Fear is a puzzle exploration game containing switches, boxes, doors and various dynamic light sources (like flashlights and lanterns) that the player uses to solve puzzles. In this game Thomas Warden searches for his lost family members (his wife Susan and his daughter Helen) through fifteen missions in a monster-ridden old hospital. He has to talk to other patients and find ways to travel deeper into the hospital.
Thomas’ most important enemy is darkness. Venturing in the dark deals damage, so he has to open windows to let the light in, find light switches or carry lanterns and flashlights. He is also able to lit fireplaces, carry mirrors and talk to other characters. There are multiple endings and the plot continues in the sequels Grim Oak and Nightmare.

The player needs to feel immersed in the game-world to be able to empathise properly with a character, and that can be difficult to pull off on a 3.5 inch screen.
Rovio, developer of Darkest Fear, has given it a good try though, despite their game being more of a puzzler than a survival horror. The game opens with history researcher Thomas Warden driving towards a hospital with the appealing name of Grim Oak’s. He has received a call from his wife Susan, a doctor at Grim Oak’s, asking him to find their autistic daughter Helen, who also happens to be a patient of a certain grim-sounding medical facility.
Of course, it isn’t as simple as checking in at reception and visiting the right ward. Thomas finds the hospital shrouded in darkness, and the problem is more substantial than a British Gas cock-up or a few flicked switches in the fuse box. The hospital’s patients have been infected with a terrible virus that transforms them into bloodthirsty monsters.

Introduction

A tribute to my childhood game...
Darkest Fear is a survival-horror puzzle game developed and published by Rovio Mobile for Java mobile phone ( J2ME ), which was released in 2005 . It is a first game in Darkest Fear game trilogy. The upgraded iPhone version was released in 2008.

Description :-

Darkest Fear defines an entirely new category of mobile games, inviting the player deep into a haunting story of hidden mystery and bitter despair. Darkest Fear features 15 challenging levels, each with its own puzzles to solve and hazards to overcome. Furniture and walls leave realistic shadows, creating an atmosphere of intense horror that test the nerves of even the most jaded player. One wrong move taken in haste is all takes for you too to get torn to pieces!

Outside

Library

The first game begins at a hospital that has been plunged into an eerie darkness. Thomas Warden is summoned to Grim Oak hospital by his wife, a doctor there. At a couple of key points, your choices and the equipment you carry make a difference to how the plot unfolds and who you can save.
Set five years after the first game, Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak gives you more monsters to evade and more light sources to take advantage of. ## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy game and Android app, improving asset management with supplied Grim Oak files and making all three chapters reflect the original games’ stories.

## Requirements
- Three chapters with four missions each.
- Support Android/mobile touch controls and desktop keyboard controls.
- Preserve the original stories across all three games.

## Decisions
- The game uses Three.js with Capacitor Android packaging and PWA support.
- The supplied JARs are alternate versions of Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak; they do not provide source material for parts 1 or 3.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented the browser game, progression, controls, PWA support, and Android Capacitor project.
- Built the debug APK at `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`.
- `npm test` and the Android debug build passed.
- Researched brief plot summaries for all three games; sources confirmed Darkest Fear’s hospital search, Grim Oak’s setting five years later, and Nightmare’s two playable characters.
- Compared JAR entry counts: first archive has 114 entries, second has 102; each has 54 PNGs.

### Active
- Compare and organize the supplied Grim Oak assets for game use.
- Verify original storylines for all three games and update game narrative and missions to match.

### Blocked
- Supplied files cover only Darkest Fear 2; original-game materials for parts 1 and 3 have not been provided, so story completeness cannot be verified from these uploads alone.

## Next Move
1. Compare the JAR contents and identify useful assets or story data; organize selected assets with clear filenames or metadata.
2. Find reliable, detailed original-story references for Darkest Fear 1 and 3; compare all three against current chapter content.
3. Update narrative and mission progression to cover the original stories, then rerun browser tests and Android builds.

## Relevant Files
- `src/main.js`: Chapter, mission, objective, and story text definitions.
- `src/world.js`: Three.js game world and gameplay implementation.
- `public/assets/df2/`: Existing Grim Oak image assets to compare with the uploaded archives.
- `README.md`: Project and build documentation.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/859b08e5-3dac-45ee-880a-9b4a212366e1/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a).jar`: First supplied Grim Oak archive.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/a9b3a233-2220-4270-85ab-7287d0d57c15/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a1).jar`: Second supplied Grim Oak archive.

## Important Context
- Current chapter content is a four-mission-per-chapter reinterpretation, not yet verified as the complete original narratives.
- Darkest Fear has fifteen original missions; Thomas searches an old hospital for wife Susan and daughter Helen.
- Grim Oak takes place five years after the first game; a GameFAQs walkthrough describes Thomas returning to a town pub where residents disbelieve him.
- Nightmare features Thomas and his daughter Helen as playable characters; Helen is affected by the dark bacteria.
- Changes remain uncommitted.

This may very well be the most enthralling, original mobile game we’ve played in 2005.
679252-929421_20050810_001.jpg Warden would probably like to wait for daybreak…but there's no time!
According to one of its cofounders, Rovio Mobile’s main axiom is to make mobile games that appeal to hardcore gamers. However, even though its first release has many exceptional features, it’s actually an entry into a pretty familiar genre: the overhead action-puzzle game. Darkest Fear tells the story of a history professor named Thomas Warden, whose wife and daughter are trapped in a darkened hospital filled with monsters. A horrible event changed most of the hospital’s patients into ravenous beings of the night, leaving the remaining occupants cowering in fear throughout the labyrinthine building’s chambers. Luckily, the monsters can survive only in total darkness, so they don’t have the full run of the place just yet; pockets of natural and artificial light–Warden’s islands of hope–remain to banish the inky blackness, fry the dread ghouls, and keep the humans alive.

...

Your standard mission is to rescue as many survivors as you can before proceeding to the next floor; although this mission is optional, each patient you save is good for an additional life point on the next level, and this becomes very important in the later, darker sections of the hospital. Rescuing a survivor involves bathing him or her in light from any of the game’s sources of luminosity, which include windows, fireplaces, flashlights, lanterns, and mirrors. Any time you step through complete darkness, you sustain damage at the rate of about one life point per second. Therefore, it’s possible to make short sacrifice-runs if absolutely necessary, but the bulk of the gameplay involves gingerly creating a path of radiance through each level.

...

because they create a circular glow. A lot of the game’s puzzles also involve more traditional elements, like keys, pressure switches, and moving boxes, and you can probably imagine how difficult they can get. In the later levels, backtracking to old, unused light sources becomes the order of the day, along with dropping them on pressure switches and carefully calculating timed runs through the dark.

## [Darkest Fear iPhone, iPod Touch Review - DarkZero](https://darkzero.co.uk/game-reviews/darkest-fear-iphone-ipod-touch)

Review August 26th 2009 Seth Bland
darkest-fear-art
Creating a truly frightening horror experience on a mobile phone is no easy feat. The player needs to feel immersed in the game-world to be able to empathise properly with a character, and that can be difficult to pull off on a 3.5 inch screen.
Rovio, developer of Darkest Fear, has given it a good try though, despite their game being more of a puzzler than a survival horror. The game opens with history researcher Thomas Warden driving towards a hospital with the appealing name of Grim Oak’s. He has received a call from his wife Susan, a doctor at Grim Oak’s, asking him to find their autistic daughter Helen, who also happens to be a patient of a certain grim-sounding medical facility.
Of course, it isn’t as simple as checking in at reception and visiting the right ward. Thomas finds the hospital shrouded in darkness, and the problem is more substantial than a British Gas cock-up or a few flicked switches in the fuse box. The hospital’s patients have been infected with a terrible virus that transforms them into bloodthirsty monsters.
darkest-fear-1

...

Keys must also be found to open other doors, but as they’re always found in one of the many wardrobes scattered about each level, this never presents much of a challenge.

...

Most levels will also feature one or more patients who can be optionally saved by making sure that the place they’re sitting in is lit up by the time you exit the level.

...

The difficulty is all over the place, with a couple of the earlier levels being much harder than the later ones. Some levels are so linear, that anything but the correct solution will result in a quick death, so you end up simply going through the obvious motions to finish the level.

...

What initially seems like it could be an intriguing plot never approaches anything interesting, and ends with a climax that makes no sense at all.
darkest-fear-4
There are two points in the game where a choice must be made, resulting in a total of three possible endings. Unfortunately none of them are interesting enough to warrant playing through all 15 levels again when you already know the solutions. One of the possible endings even sees you bypassing two ‘boss battles’ completely, meaning the levels are instantly over. This is probably for the best though, as these are the worst parts of the game anyway.

## [Darkest Fear trilogy  — Haunted Games](https://hauntedgames.net/darkest-fear-trilogy)
Published: 2023-09-14T00:00:00.000Z

safely traverse each area, save other inhabitants from a mysterious virus, and confront what nightmarish monstrosities may lie waiting in the dark.
There's also a bit of light sokobanning as you punt crates and rocks around to clear paths, and a handful of action sequences. Although some of these involve more dodging than you might necessarily like, they're rare and the games' difficulty curve is generally pretty casual.
The first game begins at a hospital that has been plunged into an eerie darkness. Thomas Warden is summoned to Grim Oak hospital by his wife, a doctor there. He finds the place shadow-haunted, deserted by its staff and, soon, haunted by hideous monsters. At a couple of key points, your choices and the equipment you carry make a difference to how the plot unfolds and who you can save.
Set five years after the first game, Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak gives you more monsters to evade and more light sources to take advantage of. There's greater emphasis on object puzzles, giving a light adventure game vibe to the proceedings. You finally get to leave the hospital and explore the town of Grim Oak.

...

The final instalment, Darkest Fear: Nightmare, introduces a second playable character who must cling to the darkness for safety as fervently Warden must keep to the light. You can switch between them to tackle puzzles suited to their unique skill-sets, and, as the overarching series narrative concludes, a total of 15 different endings can be achieved. This third entry in the series uses some particularly nice lighting effects and has generally more polished graphics.
Although the first installment was available on iOS for a while, the J2ME editions can safely be regarded as definitive. You can and should treat these as successive chapters of the same game.
Although they deal with horrific themes and bear a Mature rating, the stylised graphics leave most of the unpleasantness to your imagination.
The entire series combines a sometimes janky, yet atmospheric, plot with gratifying puzzles, solid level design, and excellent use of their target devices' limited graphical capabilities. They play nicely on modern Android devices thanks to J2ME Loader.

Darkest Fear 3: Nightmare

31.12.2006
Genre: Puzzle Adventure
Nightmare is the third and final game in the Darkest Fear trilogy and features two playable characters instead of just one in the previous games, Thomas Warden and his daughter Helen with cooperative gameplay. The game mechanics remain the same: survival horror mainly based on light sources and lots of puzzle solving, all shown from an overhead view. The game has a hidden Pong-like mini-game, 15 different endings, and Helen can obtain three unique monster abilities.
Helen has been affected the dark bacteria that forces her to stay in the dark. Thomas can stay alive by walking in places that are illuminated by various, dynamic light sources like a flashlight or a lantern. In each level the player must guide both players to the exit with as few steps as possible. They also have to find a cure for Helen's affliction. Completing the levels with good scores unlocks cheat codes.
