Published: 2023-09-14T00:00:00.000Z

There's also a bit of light sokobanning as you punt crates and rocks around to clear paths, and a handful of action sequences. Although some of these involve more dodging than you might necessarily like, they're rare and the games' difficulty curve is generally pretty casual.
The first game begins at a hospital that has been plunged into an eerie darkness. Thomas Warden is summoned to Grim Oak hospital by his wife, a doctor there. He finds the place shadow-haunted, deserted by its staff and, soon, haunted by hideous monsters. At a couple of key points, your choices and the equipment you carry make a difference to how the plot unfolds and who you can save.
Set five years after the first game, Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak gives you more monsters to evade and more light sources to take advantage of. There's greater emphasis on object puzzles, giving a light adventure game vibe to the proceedings. You finally get to leave the hospital and explore the town of Grim Oak. Graphics are more varied and the world is relatively open, giving you some choice in the order that you explore in.
The final instalment, Darkest Fear: Nightmare, introduces a second playable character who must cling to the darkness for safety as fervently Warden must keep to the light. You can switch between them to tackle puzzles suited to their unique skill-sets, and, as the overarching series narrative concludes, a total of 15 different endings can be achieved. This third entry in the series uses some particularly nice lighting effects and has generally more polished graphics.
Although the first installment was available on iOS for a while, the J2ME editions can safely be regarded as definitive. You can and should treat these as successive chapters of the same game.

## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy game and Android app, using supplied assets and aligning all three chapters with the original stories.

## Requirements
- Three chapters with four missions each.
- Support Android/mobile touch controls and desktop keyboard controls.
- Preserve the original stories across all three games.

## Decisions
- The game uses Three.js with Capacitor Android packaging and PWA support.
- Supplied archives include two alternate versions of *Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak* and one *Darkest Fear* archive; no *Nightmare* archive has been identified.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented browser gameplay, progression, controls, PWA support, and Android Capacitor project.
- Built debug APK at `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`; `npm test` and Android debug build passed.
- Researched brief plot summaries: *Darkest Fear* follows Thomas searching an old hospital for Susan and Helen; *Grim Oak* is set five years later; *Nightmare* features Thomas and Helen, who is affected by dark bacteria.
- Inspected Grim Oak archive entry lists; each contains 54 PNGs. Began inspecting MIDI/data files in the newly identified *Darkest Fear* archive.

### Active
- Compare supplied archives with existing assets and determine useful game assets or story data.
- Verify original storylines for all three games and update chapter narrative and missions accordingly.

### Blocked
- Detailed story completeness cannot yet be verified; the *Nightmare* game materials were not provided, and reference sources gathered so far are brief summaries.

## Next Move
1. Compare the three JAR archives with `public/assets/` and inspect relevant data files for usable assets or narrative details.
2. Find reliable, detailed original-story references for all three games, especially *Nightmare*.
3. Update the four-mission chapter narratives and progression to reflect the original stories, then rerun browser tests and Android build.

## Relevant Files
- `src/main.js`: Chapter, mission, objective, and story text definitions.
- `src/world.js`: Three.js world and gameplay implementation.
- `public/assets/df2/`: Existing Grim Oak image assets.
- `README.md`: Project and build documentation.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/859b08e5-3dac-45ee-880a-9b4a212366e1/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a).jar`: First supplied Grim Oak archive.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/a9b3a233-2220-4270-85ab-7287d0d57c15/Darkest Fear 2 Grim Oak (2006)(Rovio)(v1.30)(a1).jar`: Second supplied Grim Oak archive.
- `/tmp/opencode/uploads/57847857-ceb4-4910-a4b8-2ea5e794cd5d/Darkest Fear (2006)(Rovio)(v1.50)(Nokia N73, N73).jar`: Newly identified *Darkest Fear* archive.

## Important Context
- Current chapter content is a four-mission reinterpretation, not yet verified as complete original narratives; *Darkest Fear* originally has fifteen missions.
- *Grim Oak* walkthrough reference: https://gamefaqs.gamespot.com/mobile/953211-darkest-fear-2-grim-oak/faqs/79694/part-2-library
- *Nightmare* overview: https://darx.net/games/darkest-fear-3-nightmare
- Changes remain uncommitted.

<subagent sessionID="ses_e36e1d17affedkVUxXE91lznkH" state="completed">
## Review

The build has the trilogy’s broad shape—three chapters, darkness, a torch, and a pursuing monster—but currently reads as a **generic light-and-shadow survival game**, not a narrative adaptation of the trilogy. The biggest gaps are the missing family story, the setting and timeline of *Grim Oak*, and *Nightmare*’s defining two-character premise.

### Chapter I — *Darkest Fear*

The current description is “a desperate search through a haunted hospital,” but it never identifies Thomas Warden, his wife Susan, or his daughter Helen. In the original, Thomas searches for his missing family in a monster-ridden hospital. The missions—“The Hollow,” “The Ward,” “No Escape,” and “The Last Light”—and the generic three-seal objectives don’t communicate that search. The world’s props are trees, coffins, and altars rather than recognizable hospital details.  
**Recommendation:** Make Thomas’s search for Susan and Helen the chapter’s through-line, and give the four missions a clear progression through the hospital. You can convey that in the existing chapter and mission text without changing the controls or level loop. The original also has fifteen missions, so describe this four-mission version as a condensed adaptation rather than a complete mission-for-mission retelling.

### Chapter II — *Grim Oak*

The chapter is framed as a village-and-forest story: “Something has followed you into the forest.” That misses the sequel’s key context: it takes place **five years later**, follows Thomas again, and moves the story into the town of Grim Oak.  
**Recommendation:** Establish the time jump and Thomas’s return to Grim Oak, and make the missions feel like stages in exploring the town rather than a generic forest quest. Keep the four-mission format if scope requires it, but present it as a shortened chapter. The game descriptions also mention revisiting places and solving item puzzles; neither is represented by the current sequence of standalone seal-collecting levels.

### Chapter III — *Nightmare*

The current copy describes a generic nightmare and a single unnamed hero. The trilogy finale’s distinguishing feature is that Thomas and Helen are both playable and cooperate; their contrasting relationship to light and darkness is central to its premise. The current game has one player character and one torch-based survival loop, with a single “end the nightmare” objective and fixed progression.  
**Recommendation:** Decide how literally this chapter should represent *Nightmare*. If gameplay must stay as-is, frame it honestly as a condensed, single-character-inspired finale; don’t imply that it includes the original’s dual-character play or multiple endings. Story text can still make Thomas and Helen relevant, but it won’t remove that gameplay mismatch.

### Mismatches across the missions

All twelve levels use the same basic objective: collect three items and reach an exit. That is a workable core loop, but several objective labels promise actions the level does not implement—for example, “RESTORE POWER TO THE EXIT” and “END THE NIGHTMARE.” The HUD displays a seal count, and the world logic opens the exit after all three collectible items are gathered.  
**Recommendation:** Keep the existing objective-and-exit mechanic, but make the HUD objective accurately describe it. Use chapter-specific labels—seals, sigils, or shards—as flavor, and put broader story goals in chapter or mission descriptions rather than suggesting that a level has a different mechanic.

## Mechanics to preserve

The light-versus-darkness tension, torch charge, monster pressure, collectible hunt, exit gate, and linear chapter progression are all established in the current implementation. They can remain intact while the narrative text and mission framing become more specific. One important caveat: the original games use additional light sources and environmental/item puzzles, and *Nightmare* adds cooperative character differences. Keeping the current mechanics means this should be presented as a **thematic adaptation**, not a faithful recreation of those systems.

### References

- Current chapter, mission, and objective data: [`/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/src/main.js`]( /home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/src/main.js ), especially lines 7–25 and 40–43.
- Shared level layout, props, collectibles, torch, monster, and exit logic: [`/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/src/world.js`]( /home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/src/world.js ), especially lines 64–95, 97–129, and 219–259.
- README’s “three chapters and twelve missions” description: [`/home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/README.md`]( /home/runner/work/PlayGround/PlayGround/README.md ), lines 20–22.
- Trilogy background: [Darkest Fear trilogy overview](https://hauntedgames.net/darkest-fear-trilogy) and [Darkest Fear series entries](https://www.darx.net/games/darkest-fear).

No files were changed.
</subagent>

20: ## Darkest Fear — The Trilogy
21: 
22: A mobile-friendly 3D survival-puzzle game with three chapters and twelve missions. It runs in modern desktop and mobile browsers and can be installed as a home-screen web app. Progress is saved in the browser on the current device.
23: 
24: ### Run locally
25: 
26: Requirements: Node.js 20.19+ or 22.12+ and npm.
27: 
28: ```sh
29: npm install
30: npm run dev
31: ```
32: 
33: Open the local URL printed by Vite (usually `http://localhost:5173`). To build and serve the production version:
34: 
35: ```sh
36: npm run build
37: npm run preview
38: ```

43: 
44: - **Desktop:** WASD or arrow keys to move; **F** or **Space** toggles the torch; **P** or **Esc** pauses. Click a nearby floor tile to move there.
45: - **Touch:** use the on-screen directional pad and Light button, or swipe/tap the play area. Controls avoid browser swipe gestures during play.
46: - Gather all three seals in each mission, keep the torch charged, and reach the exit. The monster is repelled while illuminated.
47: 
48: Three.js renders the game locally. Google Fonts are optional; if unavailable, the interface uses system sans-serif fallbacks.
49: 
50: ### Android app
51: 
52: The Android project wraps the same offline-capable game in a native Android WebView using Capacitor. Install Android Studio (including the Android SDK and platform tools), Java 21+, then run:

56: npm run android:debug
57: ```

Install it on a connected device with `adb install -r android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`, or open the project in Android Studio with `npm run android:open` and run it on a device/emulator. To create a release APK, configure your signing credentials in Android Studio and use `npm run android:release`; the unsigned output is under `android/app/build/outputs/apk/release/`. The project requires the Android SDK platform/build tools specified in `android/variables.gradle`.

## Darkest Fear trilogy

#### Rovio, 2005-2006

Before the rise and fall of Angry Birds, Rovio produced a number of Java phone games, of which the shining jewel (or most tenebrous void?) was undoubtedly the Darkest Fear series.

Hybrid survival horror puzzle adventure games with a genuinely haunting atmosphere, the Darkest Fear games all use a top-down isometric perspective as you navigate the map and static or lightly animated photobashed cutscenes.

The primary puzzle mechanic ties in with narrative themes of (literal) darkness and light as you use illumination puzzles to safely traverse each area, save other inhabitants from a mysterious virus, and confront what nightmarish monstrosities may lie waiting in the dark.

There's also a bit of light sokobanning as you punt crates and rocks around to clear paths, and a handful of action sequences. Although some of these involve more dodging than you might necessarily like, they're rare and the games' difficulty curve is generally pretty casual.

The first game begins at a hospital that has been plunged into an eerie darkness. Thomas Warden is summoned to Grim Oak hospital by his wife, a doctor there. He finds the place shadow-haunted, deserted by its staff and, soon, haunted by hideous monsters. At a couple of key points, your choices and the equipment you carry make a difference to how the plot unfolds and who you can save.

Set five years after the first game, Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak gives you more monsters to evade and more light sources to take advantage of. There's greater emphasis on object puzzles, giving a light adventure game vibe to the proceedings. You finally get to leave the hospital and explore the town of Grim Oak. Graphics are more varied and the world is relatively open, giving you some choice in the order that you explore in.

The final instalment, Darkest Fear: Nightmare, introduces a second playable character who must cling to the darkness for safety as fervently Warden must keep to the light. You can switch between them to tackle puzzles suited to their unique skill-sets, and, as the overarching series narrative concludes, a total of 15 different endings can be achieved. This third entry in the series uses some particularly nice lighting effects and has generally more polished graphics.

Although the first installment was available on iOS for a while, the J2ME editions can safely be regarded as definitive. You can and should treat these as successive chapters of the same game.

Although they deal with horrific themes and bear a Mature rating, the stylised graphics leave most of the unpleasantness to your imagination.

The entire series combines a sometimes janky, yet atmospheric, plot with gratifying puzzles, solid level design, and excellent use of their target devices' limited graphical capabilities. They play nicely on modern Android devices thanks to J2ME Loader.

The player needs to feel immersed in the game-world to be able to empathise properly with a character, and that can be difficult to pull off on a 3.5 inch screen.
Rovio, developer of Darkest Fear, has given it a good try though, despite their game being more of a puzzler than a survival horror. The game opens with history researcher Thomas Warden driving towards a hospital with the appealing name of Grim Oak’s. He has received a call from his wife Susan, a doctor at Grim Oak’s, asking him to find their autistic daughter Helen, who also happens to be a patient of a certain grim-sounding medical facility.
Of course, it isn’t as simple as checking in at reception and visiting the right ward. Thomas finds the hospital shrouded in darkness, and the problem is more substantial than a British Gas cock-up or a few flicked switches in the fuse box. The hospital’s patients have been infected with a terrible virus that transforms them into bloodthirsty monsters.
darkest-fear-1
Like fans of Twilight, these creatures cannot abide the cold, harsh light of reality (or any other form of illumination for that matter), and so they will congregate in the shadows, ready to claw anything that enters their domain.
Luckily, Thomas can carry portable light sources like torches and lanterns, although using both hands at the same time seems to be a bit of stretch for the poor

...

behind them, instead of creating their own shadow.
Gameplay mostly consists of pushing large wooden crates onto pressure switches, which open doors. If only this was something we forced patients in all hospitals to do, we’d soon separate the hypochondriacs from the genuinely ill.

...

Some levels are so linear, that anything but the correct solution will result in a quick death, so you end up simply going through the obvious motions to finish the level.
The story is presented in stylish black-and-white static screens, and it’s a shame that the dialogue is often so awkward and forced. What initially seems like it could be an intriguing plot never approaches anything interesting, and ends with a climax that makes no sense at all.
darkest-fear-4
There are two points in the game where a choice must be made, resulting in a total of three possible endings. Unfortunately none of them are interesting enough to warrant playing through all 15 levels again when you already know the solutions. Set five years after the first game, Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak gives you more monsters to evade and more light sources to take advantage of. There's greater emphasis on object puzzles, giving a light adventure game vibe to the proceedings. You finally get to leave the hospital and explore the town of Grim Oak. Graphics are more varied and the world is relatively open, giving you some choice in the order that you explore in.
The final instalment, Darkest Fear: Nightmare, introduces a second playable character who must cling to the darkness for safety as fervently Warden must keep to the light. You can switch between them to tackle puzzles suited to their unique skill-sets, and, as the overarching series narrative concludes, a total of 15 different endings can be achieved. This third entry in the series uses some particularly nice lighting effects and has generally more polished graphics.

...

The entire series combines a sometimes janky, yet atmospheric, plot with gratifying puzzles, solid level design, and excellent use of their target devices' limited graphical capabilities. They play nicely on modern Android devices thanks to J2ME Loader.

# [Haunted Games](/)

[About](https://hauntedgames.net/about)[Links](https://hauntedgames.net/links)

## Darkest Fear trilogy

#### Rovio, 2005-2006

Before the rise and fall of Angry Birds, Rovio produced a number of Java phone games, of which the shining jewel (or most tenebrous void?) was undoubtedly the Darkest Fear series.

Hybrid survival horror puzzle adventure games with a genuinely haunting atmosphere, the Darkest Fear games all use a top-down isometric perspective as you navigate the map and static or lightly animated photobashed cutscenes.

The primary puzzle mechanic ties in with narrative themes of (literal) darkness and light as you use illumination puzzles to safely traverse each area, save other inhabitants from a mysterious virus, and confront what nightmarish monstrosities may lie waiting in the dark.

There's also a bit of light sokobanning as you punt crates and rocks around to clear paths, and a handful of action sequences. Although some of these involve more dodging than you might necessarily like, they're rare and the games' difficulty curve is generally pretty casual.

The first game begins at a hospital that has been plunged into an eerie darkness. Thomas Warden is summoned to Grim Oak hospital by his wife, a doctor there. He finds the place shadow-haunted, deserted by its staff and, soon, haunted by hideous monsters. At a couple of key points, your choices and the equipment you carry make a difference to how the plot unfolds and who you can save.

Set five years after the first game, Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak gives you more monsters to evade and more light sources to take advantage of. There's greater emphasis on object puzzles, giving a light adventure game vibe to the proceedings. You finally get to leave the hospital and explore the town of Grim Oak. Graphics are more varied and the world is relatively open, giving you some choice in the order that you explore in.

The final instalment, Darkest Fear: Nightmare, introduces a second playable character who must cling to the darkness for safety as fervently Warden must keep to the light. You can switch between them to tackle puzzles suited to their unique skill-sets, and, as the overarching series narrative concludes, a total of 15 different endings can be achieved. This third entry in the series uses some particularly nice lighting effects and has generally more polished graphics.

Although the first installment was available on iOS for a while, the J2ME editions can safely be regarded as definitive. You can and should treat these as successive chapters of the same game.

Although they deal with horrific themes and bear a Mature rating, the stylised graphics leave most of the unpleasantness to your imagination.

Walkthrough

Part 1: Pub

Pub

* You start the game at the pub. Thomas try to tell the truth to the town folks. But, they didn't believe anything that he said. When you gain control of him, read Note #1 on the table there.
* Pick up the Torch in the north-eastern room, and then drop it in point #A to light up the southern areas.
* Push the Box there onto Trigger #1 nearby to open the door.
* Open the Window in the western room to light up the way.
* Pick up the Lantern , and then drop it onto Trigger #2 (in the east) to open the door nearby.
* Pick up the Light Bulb , and then use it on another Wall Lamp in the south.
* Exit through the Back Door to get 2 Batteries . After that, re-enter the building.
* Pick up the Magnet , and then use it to get the Pub Key from the grating nearby.
* You can play SEMUA Darts mini game here if you want.
* Use the Pub Key to unlock the Front Door , and leave this place (you'll get 2 Batteries ).

Outside

Library

Introduction

Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak is a horror themed adventure-puzzle game developed and published by Rovio Mobile Ltd for Java mobile phone ( J2ME ), which was released in 2006 . It is a second game in Darkest Fear series.

Description:-

Rovio Mobile invites you to encounter your ultimate fear in Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak. It has been five years since Dr. Thomas Warden first begun unraveling the mystery behind a series of eerie events at Grim Oak's hospital. Thomas finds an exhausted patient of Grim Oak hospital. The patient reveals that all patients of the hospital, that were believed to have died in the after-treatment of a terrible disease, are alive... but dark monsters have begun lurking in the city.
Darkest Fear 2: Grim Oak brings you more dynamic lightning sources and multiple collectable objects, new challenging puzzles, and the whole city of Grim Oak to be freely explored. The painful history of Grim Oak will be revealed!

Part 11: Sheriff's Office

Outside

1. Open the inventory, and then combine the Magnet with the Rope to get the Rope with Magnet .
2. Use the Rope with Magnet to get a Dirty Sheriff's Badge from the Well .
3. Open the inventory, and then use the Soap to clean up Dirty Sheriff's Badge . You'll get a Shiny Sheriff's Badge with 4 digit number.
4. Use the Shiny Sheriff's Badge to open the door of the Sheriff's Office.
5. Enter the Sheriff's Office .

Sheriff's Office

1. Pick up the Torch #1 , and then drop it in point #A to light up the eastern areas.
2. Open the Window , and turn on the Light Switch in the north.
3. Pick up the Torch #2 , and then drop it onto Trigger #1 to light up the eastern areas.
4. Pick up the Torch #1 , and then drop it onto Trigger #2 to light up the southern areas.
5. Pick up the Candle , and then drop it onto Trigger #3 .
6. Pick up the Torch #2 , and then drop it onto Trigger #4 to light up the southern areas.
7. Pick up the Torch #1 , and then drop it onto Trigger #5 to light up the eastern areas.
8. Turn on the Light Switch in the south-east, and pick up Note #5 there.
9. Pick up the Putrid Muffin #13 in the north-eastern prison. Use Camera to light up the prison for a few seconds.
10. Use the Rope with Magnet to get the Cellar Key from behind the prison in the north-east.
11. Leave this place through the Back Door (you'll get 2 Batteries ).

Darkest Fear

Darkest Fear is a puzzle exploration game containing switches, boxes, doors and various dynamic light sources (like flashlights and lanterns) that the player uses to solve puzzles. In this game Thomas Warden searches for his lost family members (his wife Susan and his daughter Helen) through fifteen missions in a monster-ridden old hospital. He has to talk to other patients and find ways to travel deeper into the hospital.
Thomas' most important enemy is darkness. Venturing in the dark deals damage, so he has to open windows to let the light in, find light switches or carry lanterns and flashlights. He is also able to lit fireplaces, carry mirrors and talk to other characters. There are multiple endings and the plot continues in the sequels Grim Oak and Nightmare.

## Objective
- Complete the Darkest Fear trilogy game and Android app, aligning all three chapters with the original stories and supplied game materials.

## Requirements
- Three chapters with four missions each.
- Support Android/mobile touch controls and desktop keyboard controls.
- Preserve the original stories across all three games.

## Decisions
- Use Three.js with Capacitor Android packaging and PWA support.
- The supplied archives include the original *Darkest Fear*, two alternate *Grim Oak* archives, and *Nightmare*.

## Work State
### Completed
- Implemented browser gameplay, progression, controls, PWA support, and Android Capacitor project.
- Built debug APK at `android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk`; `npm test` and Android debug build passed.
- Identified all four supplied archives and compared their PNG assets with `public/assets/`; all match except one *Grim Oak* image.
- Confirmed *Darkest Fear* follows Thomas Warden searching for his wife Susan and daughter Helen through fifteen missions; *Grim Oak* is set in the town five years later.

### Active
- Verify detailed storylines and mission progression for all three chapters using the archives and reliable references.
